what the world model got wrong, the lesson. -->

+Predicted accuracy [0.746, 0.7545] and time [5.8, 6.3]; got 0.7451 and 5.70 (both slightly low). Time: I assumed a sizeable per-step fixed cost (Muon NS, optimizer, EMA, Python) that wouldn't shrink with resolution; in fact train time fell 14.6% for a 15.4% fall in pixel-weighted cost. So ~95% of train time is pixel-proportional conv work and fixed per-step overhead is only ~5%. Accuracy: the loss is ~4x the E007 resizing loss per unit of pixel saved. Two changes were confounded: the 20 px phase and the shorter full-res tail (30% -> 20%). The world model treated resolution as a smooth dial; it has a cliff. Coarse early resolution or a short 32 px tail costs a lot on 100 classes. Lesson: (1) per-step overhead work (CUDA graphs, optimizer fusion) can save at most ~5%; (2) keep >= 30% of steps at 32 px. Any further resizing should test one factor at a time (e.g. keep the tail at 30% and only add 20 px early).
<!-- the current recipe in a line or two, and its metrics -->
<!-- what dominates the objective, and why -->

+- ~95% of train time is pixel-proportional conv compute: E011 cut pixel-weighted cost 15.4% and train time fell 14.6%. Fixed per-step overhead (Muon NS, SGD, EMA, Python launch) is only ~5% -> CUDA graphs/launch work can buy at most ~0.3 s.
- E007 per-epoch train cost (compiled, Muon, bs 2000): ~0.58 s at 24 px, ~0.75 s at 28 px, ~0.93 s at 32 px (estimates from pixel scaling; total 7.22 s for 10 epochs).
- Compiled (inductor max-autotune-no-cudagraphs) + fused SGD: steady-state train 8.92 s vs 10.39 s eager at 10 epochs (-14%, ~18.6 ms/step) (E003 trials 1-2).
- E001: train ~9.30 s for 9 epochs x 48 steps = 432 steps -> ~21.5 ms/step, ~1.03 s/epoch (eager). prepare 0.07-0.2 s (first trial slower). Eval 0.1 s.
<!-- distilled from post-mortems: what went wrong, and the rule that follows -->
+- Aggressive resizing 20/24/28/32 at 30/30/20/20%: -0.97 pp for -14% time (~1.0 s/pp, worse than epochs) (E011). Confounded: 20 px phase vs shorter 32 px tail.
- Decaying LR to 0 instead of 0.07 of peak: -0.08 pp (noise) with EMA on (E009). EMA already supplies the end-of-run noise reduction; don't tune the LR floor further.
E008 (I009, H4.2.2): 9.5 epochs: acc 0.7572 (-0.18 pp), 6.98 s (-4.8%) -> supports; slope with EMA ~0.36 pp/epoch; margin 0.42 pp.
E009 (I010, H1.3.4): LR floor 0.07 -> 0: acc 0.7564 (-0.08 pp), 6.99 s -> refutes; EMA and low final LR are redundant.
E010 (I012, H1.5.2): last group 512: acc 0.7548 (-0.25 pp), 6.64 s (-4.8%) -> supports; new best but margin only +0.18 pp; need accuracy boosters next.
+E011 (I011, H2.3): 20/24/28/32 resizing: 5.70 s (-14%), acc 0.7451 (-0.97 pp) -> refutes; time ~proportional to pixels, but accuracy has a cliff with coarse/short-tail schedules.
+<!-- the current recipe in a line or two, and its metrics -->
+E010 (BEST, FEASIBLE): E008 with last group 576 -> 512. accuracy 0.7548, time 6.64 s. Margin +0.18 pp (thin; 3-seed mean noise ~0.15 pp).
+E008: E007 at 9.5 epochs (238 steps; resolution switches at 40%/70% of steps), error_on_recompile after build. accuracy 0.7572, time 6.98 s.

+E007: E006 + progressive resizing (epochs 0-3 at 24 px, 4-6 at 28 px, 7-9 at 32 px via bilinear-antialias interpolate of the augmented epoch; compile dynamic=False, each res warmed in build, build ~120 s). accuracy 0.7590, time 7.33 s.

+E006: E005 with conv filters on Muon (NS5 x3 bf16, compiled update, lr 0.24, mom 0.6, fixed-norm weights), SGD on BN biases/whiten bias/head, batch 2000 (25 steps/epoch). accuracy 0.7649, time 9.45 s.
+E005: E004 + airbench lookahead EMA (every 5 steps, alpha = 0.95^5 * (t/T)^3, final weights = EMA). accuracy 0.7583, time 9.10 s. Margin above 0.753: +0.53 pp.

+E004 (was): airbench96-style port (whiten 2x2 stem, groups 128/384/576 x3 conv, BN-GELU, Nesterov SGD lr 9 wd 0.012 bs 1024, LS 0.3, fp16 channels_last) at 10 epochs, train step torch.compile'd (max-autotune-no-cudagraphs) + fused SGD, eager eval. accuracy 0.7486, time 9.04 s. NOT feasible yet (needs >= 0.753; ~+0.45 pp short).
+<!-- what the metrics mean in practice: run-to-run noise, what a real difference looks like -->

+- Compiled training is bit-deterministic per seed (E003 == E004 per-seed accuracies). So a byte-identical re-run measures nothing; the relevant noise is how per-seed accuracy varies under any recipe perturbation (~0.2-0.6 pp per seed, i.e. ~0.15-0.35 pp on the 3-seed mean).
+- Trial 0 prepare is ~0.15 s slower than later trials (first-use allocation), ~1.7% of 9 s.
+- time = mean(prepare+train) over seeds 0,1,2; harness syncs CUDA around them. Trivial recipe costs 0.14 s, so fixed overhead is negligible.
+- Accuracy per-seed std for a ResNet9-ish recipe is ~0.25 pp (README L40 calibration, 50 trials); 3-seed mean std ~0.15 pp. Feasibility gate is 0.753 on the 3-seed mean.
+- Reference point (README): ResNet9-style, 40 epochs, width 64 -> 75.36% in 59.3 s on A100 PCIe. Our A100 SXM should be similar or a bit faster.
+<!-- what dominates the objective, and why -->

+- ~95% of train time is pixel-proportional conv compute: E011 cut pixel-weighted cost 15.4% and train time fell 14.6%. Fixed per-step overhead (Muon NS, SGD, EMA, Python launch) is only ~5% -> CUDA graphs/launch work can buy at most ~0.3 s.
+- E007 per-epoch train cost (compiled, Muon, bs 2000): ~0.58 s at 24 px, ~0.75 s at 28 px, ~0.93 s at 32 px (estimates from pixel scaling; total 7.22 s for 10 epochs).
+- Compiled (inductor max-autotune-no-cudagraphs) + fused SGD: steady-state train 8.92 s vs 10.39 s eager at 10 epochs (-14%, ~18.6 ms/step) (E003 trials 1-2).
+- E001: train ~9.30 s for 9 epochs x 48 steps = 432 steps -> ~21.5 ms/step, ~1.03 s/epoch (eager). prepare 0.07-0.2 s (first trial slower). Eval 0.1 s.
+- For a real recipe: GPU training steps (epochs x step cost). Data is 50k uint8 32x32 images (150 MB) -> GPU transfer is ~tens of ms. build() is untimed: compile/warmup there.
+<!-- each with the experiments that support it, e.g. "(E003, E007)" -->

The resulting network, called FixEfficientNet, significantly outperforms the initial architecture with the same number of parameters. For instance, our FixEfficientNet-B0 trained without additional training data achieves 79.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 5.3M parameters. This is a +0.5% absolute improvement over the Noisy student EfficientNet-B0 trained with 300M unlabeled images. An EfficientNet-L2 pre-trained with weak supervision on 300M unlabeled images and further optimized with FixRes achieves 88.5% top-1 accuracy (top-5: 98.7%), which establishes the new state of the art for ImageNet with a single crop. These improvements are thoroughly evaluated with cleaner protocols than the one usually employed for Imagenet, and particular we show that our improvement remains in the experimental setting of ImageNet-v2, that is less prone to overfitting, and with ImageNet Real Labels. In both cases we also establish the new state of the art. † † address: Facebook AI Research 1 Introduction In order to obtain the best possible performance from Convolutional neural nets (CNNs), the training and testing data distributions should match. However, in image recognition, data pre-processing procedures are often different for training and testing: the most popular practice is to extract a rectangle with random coordinates from the image to artificially increase the amount of training data. This Region of Classification (RoC) is then resized to obtain an image, or crop, of a fixed size (in pixels) that is fed to the CNN. At test time, the RoC is instead set to a square covering the central part of the image, which results in the extraction of a center crop . Thus, while the crops extracted at training and test time have the same size, they arise from different RoCs, which skews the data distribution seen by the CNN. Figure 1: Improvement brought by FixRes (in bold ) to several popular architectures from the literature. Our FixEfficientNet ( orange curve ) surpasses all EfficientNet models, including the models trained with Noisy student ( red curve ) and adversarial examples ( blue curve ). The sws models are from [ 2 ] . Tables 1 and 2 report results on larger models. Over the years, training and testing pre-processing procedures have evolved, but so far they have been optimized separately [ 3 ] . Touvron et al. show [ 1 ] that this separate optimization has a detrimental effect on the test-time performance of models. They address this problem with the FixRes method, which jointly optimizes the choice of resolutions and scales at training and test time, while keeping the same RoC sampling. We apply this method to the recent EfficientNet [ 4 ] architecture, which offers an excellent compromise between number of parameters and accuracy. This evaluation paper shows that properly combining FixRes and EfficientNet further improves the state of the art [ 4 ] . Noticeably, • We report the best performance without external data on ImageNet (top1: 85.7% ); • We report the best accuracy (top1: 88.5% ) with external data on ImageNet, and with ImageNet with Reallabels [ 5 ] ; • We achieve state-of-the-art compromises between accuracy and number of parameters, see Figure 1 ; • We validate the significance of our results on the ImageNet-v2 test set, an improved evaluation setup that clearly separates the validation and test sets. FixEfficientNet achieves the best performance. This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we introduce the corrected training procedure for EfficientNet, that produces FixEfficientNet. Section 3 analyzes our extensive evaluation and compare FixEfficientNet with the state of the art. Section 4 concludes the paper. 2 Training with FixRes: updates Recent research in image classification tends towards larger networks and higher resolution images [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . For instance, the state-of-the-art in the ImageNet ILSVRC 2012 benchmark is currently held by the EfficientNet-L2 [ 8 ] architecture with 480M parameters using 800 800 images for training. Similarly, the state-of-the-art model learned from scratch is currently EfficientNet-B8 [ 9 ] with 88M parameters using 672 672 images for training. In this note, we focus on the EfficientNet architecture [ 4 ] due to its good accuracy/cost trade-off and its popularity. Data augmentation is routinely employed at training time to improve model generalization and reduce overfitting. In this note, we use the same augmentation setup as in the original FixRes paper [ 1 ] . In addition, we have integrated label smoothing, which is orthogonal to the approach. FixRes is a very simple fine-tuning that re-trains the classifier or a few top layers at the target resolution. Therefore, it has several advantages: 1. it is computationally cheap, the back-propagation is not performed on the whole network; 2. it works with any CNN classification architecture and is complementary with the other tricks mentioned above; 3. it can be applied on a CNN that comes from a possibly non reproducible source. 3 Experiments We experiment on the ImageNet-2012 benchmark [ 10 ] , and report standard performance metrics (top-1 and top-5 accuracies) on a single image crop. 3.1 Experimental Setting We focus on the EfficientNet [ 4 ] architectures. In the literature, wo versions provide the best performance: EfficientNet trained with adversarial examples [ 9 ] , and EfficientNet trained with Noisy student [ 8 ] pre-trained in a weakly-supervised fashion on 300 million unlabeled images. We start from the EfficientNet models in rwightman’s GitHub repository [ 11 ] . These models have been converted from the original Tensorflow to PyTorch. Training. We mostly follow the FixRes [ 1 ] training protocol. The only difference is that we combine the FixRes data-augmentation with label smoothing during the fine-tuning. All our FixEfficientNets outperform the corresponding EfficientNet (see Figure 1 ). As a result and to the best of our knowledge, our FixEfficientNet-L2 surpasses all other results reported in the literature. It achieves 88.5% Top-1 accuracy and 98.7% Top-5 accuracy on the ImageNet-2012 validation benchmark [ 10 ] . Clean labels. In order to complement this evaluation, Table 3 present the results with the ImageNet clean labels proposed by Beyer et all. [ 5 ] . With 90.9% Top-1 accuracy and 98.8% Top-5 accuracy FixEfficientNet-L2 surpasses all other results reported in the literature with this labels. 3.3 Significance of the results Several runs of the same training incur variations of about 0.1 accuracy points on Imagenet due to random initialization and mini-batch sampling. In general, since the Imagenet 2012 test set is not available, most works tune the hyper-parameters on the validation set, ie. there is no distinction between validation and test set. This setting, while widely adopted, is not legitimate and can cause overfitting to go unnoticed. EfficientNets employ Neural Architecture Search, which significantly enlarges the hyper-parameter space. Additionally, the ImageNet validation images were used to filter the images from the unlabelled set [ 8 ] . Therefore the pre-trained models may benefit from more overfitting on the validation set. We quantify this in the experiments presented below. Since we use pre-trained EfficientNet for our initialization, our results are comparable to those from the Noisy Student [ 8 ] , which uses the same degree of overfitting, but not directly with other semi-supervised approaches like that of Yalniz et al. [ 2 ] . Figure 2: Evidence of overfitting on Imagenet-val: We compare the results obtained on ImageNet (x-axis) and the results obtained on ImageNet-v2 (y-axis), without FixRes for different models [ 12 , 13 , 8 , 14 , 15 , 2 , 16 , 1 ] . For a given performance on Imagenet-val, overfitted models tend to have a lower performance on ImageNet-v2 and therefore are below the approaches that generalize better. 3.4 Evaluation on ImageNet-V2 The ImageNet-V2 [ 17 ] dataset was introduced to overcome the lack of a test split in the Imagenet dataset. ImageNet-V2 consists of 3 novel test sets that replace the ImageNet test set, which is no longer available. They were carefully designed to match the characteristics of the original test set. One of these test sets, Matched Frequency is the closest to the ImageNet validation set. To ensure that observed improvements are not due to overfitting, we evaluate all our models on the Matched Frequency version of the ImageNet-v2 [ 17 ] dataset. We evaluate the other methods in the same way. We present the results in Tables 4 and 5 . The original study of [ 17 ] shows that there is significant overfitting of various models to the Imagenet 2012 valuation set, but that it does not impact the relative order of the models. Quantifying the overfitting on Imagenet. As mentioned earlier, several choices in the Noisy Student [ 8 ] method are prone to overfitting. We verify this hypothesis and quantify its extent by comparing the relative accuracy of this approach with another semi-supervised approach [ 2 ] both on ImageNet and ImageNet-V2 [ 17 ] . Without overfitting, models performing similarly on Imagenet should also have similar performances on ImageNet-V2 [ 17 ] . However, for a comparable performance on ImageNet, when evaluating on ImageNet-V2, the Billion scale models of Yalniz et al. [ 2 ] outperform the EfficientNets from Noisy Student. For example, FixResNeXt-101 32x4d [ 1 ] has the same performance as EfficientNet-B3 [ 8 ] on ImageNet but on ImageNet-V2 FixResNeXt-101 32x4d [ 1 ] is better (+0.7% Top-1 accuracy). This shows that the EfficientNet Noisy student [ 8 ] tends to overfit and does not generalize as well as the (prior) semi-supervised work [ 2 ] or other works of the literature. Figure 2 illustrates this effect. The FixRes fine-tuning procedure is neutral with respect to overfitting: overfitted models remain overfitted and conversely. Comparison with the state of the art. Despite overfitting, EfficientNet remains very competitive on ImageNet-V2, as reported in Table 6 . Interestingly, the FixEfficientNet-L2 that we fine-tuned from EfficientNet establishes the new state of the art with additional data on this benchmark. That is the only way to buy back 0.5-1 epoch."]}","structured_output":{"world_model":"W1 (mechanism), after E012.

The setup
- The tip is E010: E008 (Muon on the conv filters, Lookahead/EMA, resizing 24/28/32 at 40/30/30%, batch 2000, 9.5 nominal epochs, 238 steps) with group 3 narrowed to 512 channels.
- It scores 6.639 s and 0.75477, a margin of 0.18 pp over 0.753.
- E012 reran the tip bit-identically. It reports no held-out seed data, so whether seeds 0-2 sit high is still open.

Measured effects
- Compile + fused SGD: −14% time, deterministic accuracy (E003 = E004 to the digit; E010 = E012).
- Lookahead/EMA: +0.97 pp at about 0.6% time (E005).
- LR floor 0.07 → 0: −0.08 pp. It is redundant with the EMA anneal (E009).
- Muon: +0.66 pp at +4% time (E006).
- Resizing 24/28/32: −22% time, −0.59 pp (E007).
- 0.5 epoch cut: −0.18 pp, −4.8% time (E008).
- Width 576 → 512: −4.8% time, −0.25 pp (E010).
- Resizing with a 20 px stage (E011): −22% time, −0.97 pp. At 20 px the group-3 maps shrink to 2×2, so features degrade much faster than FLOPs fall. Resolution has hit its floor.

The time model
- Fixed cost is about 0.4 s: H2D copy, eigh, pad, the per-epoch 25-way masked-copy augment (host syncs), and the interpolate.
- The variable part is about 6.2 s, GPU-bound at about 26 ms per step. The Muon update is already compiled and its lr is a GPU tensor. The SGD lr is a Python float on the fused SGD, which is outside the compile, so it causes no recompiles.
- Systems-only levers (CUDA graphs, removing graph breaks, folding the augment into the compiled region) are worth 0-4% at most. Max-autotune variants risk slowdowns or memory-pool blowup across 3 resolutions (E003-style).
- Real time tracks pixel share slightly better than linearly.

The accuracy model
- Effects of averaging and optimizer changes are larger than my priors (E005, E006). Simple dial effects (epochs, width) land near the central forecast.
- Muon renormalizes the conv weights and its update has no weight decay term. So weight decay acts only on the BN biases and the head, and "halving wd" for Muon is a no-op; expect ±0.2 pp.
- Muon lr sets the angular step size. A ×1.5 change with 238 steps and EMA damping could move accuracy either way by about 0.3 pp; slightly negative is likely.
- The Lookahead reset damps the variance of the fast weights. A plain EMA with a short final window (about 20 steps) probably loses 0.1-0.5 pp.
- Exchange rates for buying time with accuracy: about 0.36 pp per 10% time (epochs), about 0.5 pp per 10% (width), and about 0.27 pp per 10% (moderate resizing), with a sharp cliff past it.

The setup
- The tip is E010: Muon on the conv filters, Lookahead/EMA, resizing 24/28/32 px at 40/30/30% of steps, batch 2000, 9.5 nominal epochs (about 238 steps), widths 128/384/512.

- Compile + fused SGD: −14% time, deterministic (E003/E004).
- Lookahead/EMA: +0.97 pp for about 0.6% time (E005).

- Cutting 0.5 epoch: −0.18 pp, −4.8% time (E008).
- Width 576→512: −0.25 pp, −4.8% time (E010).
- Flat retunes:
  - LR floor 0.07→0: −0.08 pp (E009);
  - label smoothing 0.3→0.2: about 0 (E013);
  - Muon lr 0.24→0.36: about 0 (E014).
- So the large wins came from structural changes (averaging, the optimizer, resolution, compile). Scalar retunes near the airbench values are flat within ±0.1 pp, and I now give a ≥0.3 pp scalar retune a prior of about 10%.

Weight decay
- In the code, muon_update has no weight-decay term, and Muon renormalizes the filters to a fixed norm.
- So weight decay reaches only the BatchNorm biases, the whitening bias and the head. Halving it changes the dynamics very little: about ±0.15 pp, expected about 0.

Time model
- Fixed cost is about 0.4 s: the host-to-GPU copy, the eigendecomposition, the pad, and the augment, which does 25 boolean-mask copies per epoch, each with a nonzero host sync (about 250 syncs in all), plus the interpolate.
- Training is GPU-bound at about 26 ms per step at batch 2000. Launch overhead is a few percent at most.
- CUDA graphs or graph-break removal would save about 0.05-0.2 s (1-3%), mostly by removing the augment syncs and the Python LR loop.
- Capturing with max-autotune cudagraphs across 3 resolutions plus the Muon/EMA state risks recapture, memory-pool or compile-leak costs, as in E003. That makes the time distribution skew high.

- Endpoint averaging matters a lot. The alpha ramp (0.95^5·(k/T)^3) means the EMA tracks the live weights early and averages over about 20 steps at the end.
- The Lookahead reset also damps fast-weight noise during training at the 0.07 LR floor.
- A plain EMA keeps most of the gain but probably loses 0.1-0.4 pp.
- Exchange rates for buying time with accuracy:
  - epochs: about 0.37 pp per 10% time;
  - width: about 0.5 pp per 10%;
  - moderate resizing: about 0.27 pp per 10%, with a cliff.

- Accuracy is bit-identical per recipe; time repeats within 1%.

- How large the augment and host stall really is under the 4-CPU pin.
- Whether the remaining structural levers can buy margin to spend on epochs: dropping the head bias or scaling, a different BN momentum, a better EMA schedule, or a whitening variant.

# D002: What mechanism explains this result, which none of our forecasters predicted? Experiment E011: Exploit, building on E007's finding that time scales with pixel count. On the E007 recipe at 9 epochs, use a more aggressive resolution schedule: the first 30% of steps at 20 px, then 30% at 24 px, 20% at 28 px, and the last 20% at 32 px. Each resolution is compiled and warmed up in build with chann Measured time=5.703121792665722, accuracy=0.7451; forecast ranges were W1 {'time': [5.75, 6.1, 6.5], 'accuracy': [0.7465, 0.7525, 0.757]}; W2 {'time': [5.9, 6.5, 7.1], 'accuracy': [0.748, 0.7545, 0.7595]}; W3 {'time': [5.95, 6.3, 6.75], 'accuracy': [0.7465, 0.7515, 0.756]}; W4 {'time': [5.9, 6.6

Request R002 (committee, after E011); 80 papers found, 10 relevant, 5 read in full, 14 verified claims; cost $0.69

**Digest: E011 (20→24→28→32 px) came in faster and less accurate than all four forecasts predicted**

**The result.** E011 ran in 5.70 s, below every forecaster's low bound. Accuracy was 0.7451, also below every low bound. So the schedule gave more speed than expected and cost more accuracy than expected.

**Accuracy: the network gets too little time at full resolution.** The FixRes papers explain the accuracy shortfall best.
- **C0009 and C0013:** if training sees objects at a different apparent size than testing does, accuracy drops. Here, downscaling the whole image to 20 or 24 px shrinks objects in pixel terms. The test set is always 32 px, and the global max-pool head has to bridge that gap.
- **C0011:** a short phase of fine-tuning at the test resolution recovers the lost accuracy. That phase is what E011 cut: 30% of steps at 32 px in E007, only 20% in E011. With the LR and EMA averaging both running over a shorter full-resolution stretch, the weights and BatchNorm statistics probably adapt less to 32 px.
- **Status:** C0011 *explains* the result. This mechanism, not "fewer pixels overall", is what the tree's H2.3 should be about.
- **Next step:** keep the 20/24 px start but restore the 32 px phase to 30% or more. Separately, test recalibrating BatchNorm stats at 32 px (H1.3.6).
- **Caveat:** the FixRes evidence comes from ImageNet with pretrained or fine-tuned models, so the size of the effect here is *conditional*.

**A mechanism the tree lacks.**
- **C0019 and C0020 (EfficientNetV2):** progressive resizing on its own lowers accuracy. The fix is to scale regularization with image size: weaker augmentation and dropout at small sizes, stronger at large sizes.
- Our recipe applies the same regularization at every size: label smoothing 0.3, crop augmentation and alternating flip. At 20 px that likely over-regularizes, which would explain why the accuracy loss grew faster than the forecasters expected.
- **Status:** *untested* here.
- **Next step:** add an H2.3 child that lowers label smoothing (and/or crop strength) in the low-resolution phases and keeps it at 0.3 at 32 px. Compare against E011 at the same time cost.

**Time: why it beat the pixel-count model.** None of the cards explains the extra speed.
- If time scaled with pixel count, E011 would take about 0.847 of E007's time (654 vs 773 pixel-units per sample), or about 6.2 s.
- It measured 5.70 s, which is more than proportional. If there were a fixed per-step overhead, the speedup would be *less* than proportional, so this hints that very small feature maps are especially cheap per pixel (for example, better cache use or a different kernel choice).
- **C0016** only says in general terms that training at reduced resolution is efficient.
- **Next step:** profile time per step at each resolution before forecasting the next schedule. Don't assume a linear pixel model.

**Not relevant.**
- **C0007 and C0008:** fine-tuning on high-resolution x-rays (128–900 px). Their wall-time conclusion runs the opposite way to ours and has no bearing here.
- **C0012, C0014, C0015, C0017 and C0018:** these address test-resolution increases, overfitting, normalization type and group convolutions. None of them touches E011.

**What this means for the tree.** The literature backs E011's discard. It suggests the accuracy budget should go to a longer final phase at 32 px rather than to an even more aggressive start. It also suggests adding size-dependent regularization as a new mechanism under H2.3.

## Claims
- C0011 (explains; H2.3, H2.3.1): E011 cut the 32 px phase from 30% to 20% of steps, leaving too little time to adapt to the test resolution. Next: keep the low-resolution start but restore the 32 px tail to 30% or more.
- C0009 (explains; H2.3): A mismatch between the object sizes seen in training and at test lowers accuracy. Downscaling whole images to 20 px widens that mismatch for the max-pool head. Recast H2.3 around this mismatch rather than total FLOPs.
- C0013 (conditional; H2.3): Shows how sampling differences cause the train/test mismatch. The evidence is from ImageNet RandomResizedCrop, so the effect size here is uncertain.

On the E007 recipe at 9 epochs, use a more aggressive resolution schedule: the first 30% of steps at 20 px, then 30% at 24 px, 20% at 28 px, and the last 20% at 32 px. Request R002 (committee, after E011); 80 papers found, 10 relevant, 5 read in full, 14 verified claims; cost $0.69

**Digest: E011 (20→24→28→32 px) came in faster and less accurate than all four forecasts predicted**

**The result.** E011 ran in 5.70 s, below every forecaster's low bound. Accuracy was 0.7451, also below every low bound. So the schedule gave more speed than expected and cost more accuracy than expected.

**Accuracy: the network gets too little time at full resolution.** The FixRes papers explain the accuracy shortfall best.
- **C0009 and C0013:** if training sees objects at a different apparent size than testing does, accuracy drops. Here, downscaling the whole image to 20 or 24 px shrinks objects in pixel terms. The test set is always 32 px, and the global max-pool head has to bridge that gap.
- **C0011:** a short phase of fine-tuning at the test resolution recovers the lost accuracy. That phase is what E011 cut: 30% of steps at 32 px in E007, only 20% in E011. With the LR and EMA averaging both running over a shorter full-resolution stretch, the weights and BatchNorm statistics probably adapt less to 32 px.
- **Status:** C0011 *explains* the result. This mechanism, not "fewer pixels overall", is what the tree's H2.3 should be about.
- **Next step:** keep the 20/24 px start but restore the 32 px phase to 30% or more. Separately, test recalibrating BatchNorm stats at 32 px (H1.3.6).
- **Caveat:** the FixRes evidence comes from ImageNet with pretrained or fine-tuned models, so the size of the effect here is *conditional*.

**A mechanism the tree lacks.**
- **C0019 and C0020 (EfficientNetV2):** progressive resizing on its own lowers accuracy. The fix is to scale regularization with image size: weaker augmentation and dropout at small sizes, stronger at large sizes.
- Our recipe applies the same regularization at every size: label smoothing 0.3, crop augmentation and alternating flip. At 20 px that likely over-regularizes, which would explain why the accuracy loss grew faster than the forecasters expected.
- **Status:** *untested* here.
- **Next step:** add an H2.3 child that lowers label smoothing (and/or crop strength) in the low-resolution phases and keeps it at 0.3 at 32 px. Compare against E011 at the same time cost.

**Time: why it beat the pixel-count model.** None of the cards explains the extra speed.
- If time scaled with pixel count, E011 would take about 0.847 of E007's time (654 vs 773 pixel-units per sample), or about 6.2 s.
- It measured 5.70 s, which is more than proportional. If there were a fixed per-step overhead, the speedup would be *less* than proportional, so this hints that very small feature maps are especially cheap per pixel (for example, better cache use or a different kernel choice).
- **C0016** only says in general terms that training at reduced resolution is efficient.
- **Next step:** profile time per step at each resolution before forecasting the next schedule. Don't assume a linear pixel model.

**Not relevant.**
- **C0007 and C0008:** fine-tuning on high-resolution x-rays (128–900 px). Their wall-time conclusion runs the opposite way to ours and has no bearing here.
- **C0012, C0014, C0015, C0017 and C0018:** these address test-resolution increases, overfitting, normalization type and group convolutions. None of them touches E011.

**What this means for the tree.** The literature backs E011's discard. It suggests the accuracy budget should go to a longer final phase at 32 px rather than to an even more aggressive start. It also suggests adding size-dependent regularization as a new mechanism under H2.3.

python research.py idea next | head -1 | cut -c1-60 && cat > /tmp/diag_prof.py <<'EOF'
# Dev diagnostic on random data: GPU busy fraction over a full trial, plus sync counts.
import importlib.util, sys, time, torch
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/jovyan/work/arena3/hypothesis-unc")
from benchmark.api import BuildContext, TrainingData
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("sub", sys.argv[1])
sub = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); sys.modules["sub"] = sub; spec.loader.exec_module(sub)
dev = torch.device("cuda")
state = sub.build(BuildContext(dev, {}))
data = TrainingData(torch.randint(0, 256, (50000, 3, 32, 32), dtype=torch.uint8), torch.randint(0, 100, (50000,)))
sub.prepare(state, data, 0); sub.train(state); torch.cuda.synchronize()
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity
with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof:
    t = time.time(); sub.prepare(state, data, 1); torch.cuda.synchronize(); tp = time.time() - t
    t = time.time(); sub.train(state); torch.cuda.synchronize(); tt = time.time() - t
print(f"prepare {tp:.3f}s train {tt:.3f}s")
ev = [e for e in prof.events() if e.device_type == torch.autograd.DeviceType.CUDA]
busy = sum(e.time_range.elapsed_us() for e in ev) / 1e6
print(f"sum of GPU kernel time {busy:.3f}s over wall {tp+tt:.3f}s -> {busy/(tp+tt):.1%} (overlaps ignored)")
tab = prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cuda_time_total", row_limit=25)
print(tab)
syncs = [e for e in prof.key_averages() if any(k in e.key for k in ("cudaStreamSynchronize", "cudaDeviceSynchronize", "cudaMemcpyAsync", "nonzero", "item", "_local_scalar_dense"))]
for e in syncs: print("SYNC-ish", e.key, e.count, f"{e.cpu_time_total/1e3:.1f}ms cpu")
EOF

# Dev diagnostic on random data: GPU busy fraction over a full trial, plus sync counts.
import importlib.util, sys, time, torch
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/jovyan/work/arena3/hypothesis-unc")
from benchmark.api import BuildContext, TrainingData
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("sub", sys.argv[1])
sub = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); sys.modules["sub"] = sub; spec.loader.exec_module(sub)
dev = torch.device("cuda")
state = sub.build(BuildContext(dev, {}))
data = TrainingData(torch.randint(0, 256, (50000, 3, 32, 32), dtype=torch.uint8), torch.randint(0, 100, (50000,)))
sub.prepare(state, data, 0); sub.train(state); torch.cuda.synchronize()
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity
with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof:
    t = time.time(); sub.prepare(state, data, 1); torch.cuda.synchronize(); tp = time.time() - t
    t = time.time(); sub.train(state); torch.cuda.synchronize(); tt = time.time() - t
print(f"prepare {tp:.3f}s train {tt:.3f}s")
ev = [e for e in prof.events() if e.device_type == torch.autograd.DeviceType.CUDA]
busy = sum(e.time_range.elapsed_us() for e in ev) / 1e6
print(f"sum of GPU kernel time {busy:.3f}s over wall {tp+tt:.3f}s -> {busy/(tp+tt):.1%} (overlaps ignored)")
tab = prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cuda_time_total", row_limit=25)
print(tab)
syncs = [e for e in prof.key_averages() if any(k in e.key for k in ("cudaStreamSynchronize", "cudaDeviceSynchronize", "cudaMemcpyAsync", "nonzero", "item", "_local_scalar_dense"))]
for e in syncs: print("SYNC-ish", e.key, e.count, f"{e.cpu_time_total/1e3:.1f}ms cpu")
EOF

cp submissions/arena/submission.py drafts/I021.submission.py && python - <<'EOF'
p='drafts/I021.submission.py'
s=open(p).read()
old=s[s.index('def augment('):s.index('class Lookahead')]
new='''def augment(padded, flip_mask, epoch, translate):
    """Random crop (from reflect-padded images) plus derandomized alternating flip, sync-free."""
    n, c, hp, wp = padded.shape
    h, w = hp - 2 * translate, wp - 2 * translate
    device = padded.device
    dy = torch.randint(0, 2 * translate + 1, (n, 1), device=device)
    dx = torch.randint(0, 2 * translate + 1, (n, 1), device=device)
    rows = (dy + torch.arange(h, device=device)).view(n, 1, h, 1).expand(n, c, h, wp)
    out = padded.gather(2, rows)
    flip = flip_mask if epoch % 2 == 0 else ~flip_mask
    # A flipped crop reads columns right to left.
    cols = torch.arange(w, device=device).expand(n, w)
    cols = torch.where(flip.view(n, 1), w - 1 - cols, cols) + dx
    return out.gather(3, cols.view(n, 1, 1, w).expand(n, c, h, w))


'''
s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)

content.thinking: Since `augment` was the only change and offline checks show identical crop/flip distributions, the E016 gain could just be trajectory noise or a lucky seed rather than a real effect. I'll use idle GPU time to rerun E016 and E017 on seeds 3–12 to confirm which it is.

import json,statistics as st
a=[json.loads(l)['accuracy'] for l in open('$d/trials.jsonl')]
t=[json.loads(l)['total_timed_time'] for l in open('$d/trials.jsonl')]
print(a); print('mean %.4f std %.4f time %.3f'%(st.mean(a),st.stdev(a),st.mean(t)))"; done

content.text: Held-out mean is 0.7531 (−0.25 pp) for only −0.13 s, about 0.5 s/pp. That refutes the regime hypothesis, and 26 px kernels turned out inefficient. Discarding.

python research.py log --status discard --verdict refutes 2>&1 | tail -3 && git reset -q --hard $(git log --format=%h -1 HEAD~1) && git log --oneline -1 && python - <<'EOF'
p='notebook/E024.md'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace("<!-- After the run: the numbers, which contingency fired, the verdict and why. -->\n",
"<!-- After the run: the numbers, which contingency fired, the verdict and why. -->\nseeds 0-2: 0.7510 (0.7492 / 0.7529 / 0.7510), time 6.07 s (-2.0% vs E023; I modelled -4.4%). Infeasible -> discarded. Held-out 3-12: 0.7545 0.7539 0.7546 0.7537 0.7509 0.7535 0.7550 0.7543 0.7503 0.7501 -> mean 0.7531, -0.25 pp vs E023 (0.7556). Rate 0.13 s / 0.25 pp ~ 0.5 s/pp, far worse than epochs -> refutes the feature-map-regime child: staying in the 3x3 final-map regime does not make lower resolution cheap in accuracy. The time saving was half the pixel model: 26 px gives odd map sizes (25/12/6) that tile poorly.\n",1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
p='world_model.md'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace("_Last updated after: E023_","_Last updated after: E024_")
s=s.replace("## Dead ends\n","## Dead ends\n- Middle phase 28 -> 26 px: -2% time (half the pixel model; odd map sizes tile poorly) for -0.25 pp held-out (~0.5 s/pp) (E024). The resolution schedule 24/28/32 at 40/30/30 is a local optimum; every change tried (E011, E018, E024) has a worse rate than epochs.\n")
s=s.replace("E023 (9.0 ep, tip) 0.7556.","E023 (9.0 ep, tip) 0.7556, E024 (26 px mid) 0.7531.")
s=s.rstrip("\n")+"\nE024 (I037, H2.3): 26 px middle phase: 6.07 s (-2%), held-out 0.7531 (-0.25 pp) -> refutes; resolution schedule is at a local optimum.\n"
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
python research.py snapshot; python research.py idea next | head -1 | cut -c1-900

class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes, widths, bn_momentum, scaling_factor):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer("mean", torch.tensor(CIFAR_MEAN).view(1, 3, 1, 1))
        self.register_buffer("std", torch.tensor(CIFAR_STD).view(1, 3, 1, 1))
        whiten_width = 2 * 3 * 2 * 2
        self.whiten = nn.Conv2d(3, whiten_width, kernel_size=2, padding=0, bias=True)
        self.whiten.weight.requires_grad = False
        self.groups = nn.Sequential(
            ConvGroup(whiten_width, widths[0], bn_momentum),
            ConvGroup(widths[0], widths[1], bn_momentum),
            ConvGroup(widths[1], widths[2], bn_momentum),
        )
        self.head = nn.Linear(widths[2], num_classes, bias=False)

s=s.replace("""- If it lands in the predicted range:

- If it moves the opposite way: discard.
- If it crashes: grad-None handling in fused SGD / Muon (offline check passed).""")
s=s.replace("## In-flight notes\n","## In-flight notes\n- Offline 2-epoch check (random data): 1.248 s vs 1.367 s base for 12 frozen 32 px steps -> ~10 ms saved per frozen step (~28% of a 32 px step), much more than my FLOP estimate (~13%): group 1 backward on 31x31/15x15 maps is memory-bound (BN/GELU/residual grads at the largest maps). open(p,'w').write(s)

Re-timing the warm-up length and peak position (and the EMA start) relative to the resolution schedule raises accuracy per epoch at zero time cost.
  H1 supported c=0.85: The number of epochs needed to reach 75% (sample efficiency) sets most of the wall time. Backbone, optimizer and regularization choices that cut epochs-to-target are the main lever. Together with resizing and compile, they give about 10x over the 40-epoch ResNet9 baseline (59.3 s → 6.02 s at E026).

Group-1 conv filters, the whitening bias and group-1 BN params get their own param groups. Their LR follows the global triangle to its peak, then decays linearly to 0 at 75% of total steps. The resolution phases (20/24/28/32 at 15/25/30/30%), the freeze point (75%), and the LR and Lookahead schedules stay fixed fractions of the new total. Capture full and truncated 32 px variants in build with channels_last synthetic tensors, with error_on_recompile on. In the same session, run held-out seeds 3–12. Keep if seeds 0–2 ≥ 0.753 and held-out ≥ 0.7545. Do not re-roll RNG streams to chase seeds 0–2.

Held-out mean about 0.7540–0.7555 (E028's 0.7525 plus 0.5 epoch × 0.37–0.44 pp/epoch). Seeds 0–2 clear 0.753 with about 60–75% probability. If held-out is below 0.7535, the freeze has a hidden cost at the longer schedule; then try 9.5 epochs only if it still projects under 5.85 s.

The whitening layer and group 1 change little late in training, and their backward on the largest maps is memory-bound. E028 froze group 1 and the whitening bias for the last 25% of steps and saved ~9.5 ms per 32 px step (~27%). Air bench (whitening bias trained for 3 epochs only, 'without reducing accuracy'), Hiverge (whitening bias trained for the first 20% of steps) and FreezeOut (~20% saving with no loss on ResNets/WRNs, including CIFAR-100) are published precedents. content.thinking: The profile confirms H6.3.1: conv kernels take ~66%, Triton BN/GELU/pointwise 27%, and the frozen-stem step saves 7.7ms (nearly half from the memory-bound Triton kernels). The no-change rerun scored 0.7497, so across builds the tip has ranged 0.7532/0.7525/0.7497—meaning it only clears the local bar on favorable builds.

p='notebook/E043.md'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace("<!-- After the run: the numbers, which contingency fired, the verdict and why. -->
",
"<!-- After the run: the numbers, which contingency fired, the verdict and why. -->
ar.py no-change re-run of E036: seeds 0-2 0.7497 (0.7518 / 0.7469 / 0.7503), 5.29 s. Across three builds the tip read 0.7532 (E036), 0.7525 (E038), 0.7497 (E043): build-to-build spread on the seeds 0-2 mean is ~0.35 pp here (larger than E019's +-0.03), so the tip clears the local bar only on a favourable build. Population (20 seeds): 0.7547.
Offline profile (synthetic data, batch 2000, 10 steps each, GPU kernel time per step):
| step | total | conv fwd | conv wgrad | conv dgrad | triton fused (BN/GELU/pointwise/reductions) | aten misc | GEMM (Muon NS + head) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 32 px full (whitening detached) | 33.5 ms | 7.6 (23%) | 8.0 (24%) | 6.4 (19%) | 9.2 (27%) | 1.0 (3%) | 0.85 (2.5%) |
| 32 px frozen stem | 25.8 ms | 7.6 (30%) | 6.5 (25%) | 3.8 (15%) | 5.7 (22%) | 1.0 (4%) | 0.72 (3%) |
| 24 px full | 18.7 ms | 3.9 (21%) | 4.2 (23%) | 3.2 (17%) | 5.2 (28%) | 1.0 (5%) | 0.82 (4%) |
Supports H6.3.1: non-GEMM work is ~31% of the 32 px full step. The stem freeze saves 7.7 ms/step: dgrad -2.6, wgrad -1.5, triton -3.5 ms, so nearly half its gain is memory-bound fused kernels. Muon NS is small (~0.8 ms/step, ~2.5%). Remaining levers: the fused BN/GELU kernels (27%) are memory-bound and could shrink with fewer BN layers or cheaper activations (e.g. ReLU, or dropping a BN in the residual path); the convs are ~2/3 and run on cuDNN/Triton templates. Logged as discard (no change).
",1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
p='world_model.md'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace("_Last updated after: E042_","_Last updated after: E043_")
s=s.replace("- Per-epoch train cost on E010","- Kernel-class profile (E043, 32 px full step 33.5 ms GPU): conv fwd 23%, wgrad 24%, dgrad 19%, fused triton BN/GELU/pointwise 27%, aten misc 3%, Muon/head GEMMs 2.5%. Frozen-stem step 25.8 ms. 24 px step 18.7 ms. Non-GEMM ~31% -> BN/activation memory traffic is a real lever.
- Per-epoch train cost on E010")
s=s.replace("- Winner's curse: on the tip E036,","- Build-to-build spread of the seeds 0-2 mean for the E036 recipe: 0.7532 / 0.7525 / 0.7497 (E036/E038/E043) -> ~0.35 pp. The tip clears the local bar only on favourable builds; population mean 0.7547 (20 seeds).
- Winner's curse: on the tip E036,")
s=s.rstrip("
")+"
E043 (I058, H6.3.1): profile: non-GEMM ~31% of 32 px step, triton BN/GELU 27%, Muon 2.5%; rerun seeds 0-2 0.7497 -> supports; tip is at the local edge.
"
open(p,'w').write(s)

# Isolated fp16 channels_last conv timings (fwd, and bwd = dgrad + wgrad) at batch 2000.
import torch, time
torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True
dev = "cuda"
def bench(cin, cout, hw, n=2000, reps=20):
    x = torch.randn(n, cin, hw, hw, device=dev, dtype=torch.half).contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last).requires_grad_(True)
    conv = torch.nn.Conv2d(cin, cout, 3, padding=1, bias=False).to(dev).half().to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    for _ in range(3):
        y = conv(x); y.backward(torch.ones_like(y))
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    t = time.time()
    for _ in range(reps): y = conv(x)
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); tf = (time.time() - t) / reps
    g = torch.ones_like(y)
    t = time.time()
    for _ in range(reps):
        y = conv(x); y.backward(g)
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); tfb = (time.time() - t) / reps
    flops = 2 * n * hw * hw * cin * cout * 9
    return tf * 1e3, (tfb - tf) * 1e3, flops / tf / 1e12, 2 * flops / (tfb - tf) / 1e12

Compare per-seed accuracies across the two builds and record mean time against the E036 build. (3) Keep max-autotune with cudagraphs, but pin kernel choice by persisting the inductor/autotune cache under submissions/arena/. Populate it from a synthetic-data build only, never real data. Do two fresh-process builds that read the pinned cache and compare per-seed accuracies. First check RULES.md and the submission contract to confirm that a shipped compile cache is allowed. If it is not, report arm (3) as diagnostic only. Commit only if arm (2) or arm (3) is bit-identical across rebuilds at ≤0.5% time cost versus E036. In that case it becomes the deterministic baseline, and every later idea compares seeds 0–2 and 13–32 against it exactly.

Do two fresh-process builds that read the pinned cache and compare per-seed accuracies. First check RULES.md and the submission contract to confirm that a shipped compile cache is allowed. If it is not, report arm (3) as diagnostic only. Commit only if arm (2) or arm (3) is bit-identical across rebuilds at ≤0.5% time cost versus E036. In that case it becomes the deterministic baseline, and every later idea compares seeds 0–2 and 13–32 against it exactly.
expected: (1) Bit-identical, about 85% likely. (2) Bit-identical across rebuilds, about 70% likely, at +0.3 to +1.0% time (E015's cudagraph gain was −0.9%). If (1) fails, nondeterministic kernels cause the spread, pinning cannot help, and every comparison must stay at 20 seeds per arm. Time objective: change between −0.2% and +1%, so this is not expected to produce a new best by itself.

p='drafts/I080.submission.py'
s=open(p).read()
def rep(a,b):
    global s
    assert a in s, a
    s=s.replace(a,b)

        super().__init__(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding="same", bias=False)''','''class Conv(nn.Conv2d):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, stride=1):
        padding = "same" if stride == 1 else 0
        super().__init__(in_channels, out_channels, 3, stride=stride, padding=padding, bias=False)''')
rep('''    def __init__(self, channels_in, channels_out, bn_momentum):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = Conv(channels_in, channels_out)
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2)''','''    def __init__(self, channels_in, channels_out, bn_momentum, strided=False):
        super().__init__()
        # strided: a 3x3 stride-2 conv replaces conv + 2x2 max-pool (same output size for odd inputs).
        self.conv1 = Conv(channels_in, channels_out, stride=2 if strided else 1)
        self.pool = nn.Identity() if strided else nn.MaxPool2d(2)''')
rep('''            ConvGroup(whiten_width, widths[0], bn_momentum),''','''            ConvGroup(whiten_width, widths[0], bn_momentum, strided=True),''')
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

    total_steps = sum(pass_steps)''')

        epoch_images = augment(state.padded, state.flip_mask, epoch, hyp["translate"])

    for epoch, epoch_len in enumerate(pass_steps):

                step >= g2_step,
            )
            step += 1''','''            losses = train_step(
                model, opt, x, y, hyp["label_smoothing"], step >= freeze_step, step >= whiten_bias_steps,
                step >= g2_step,
            )
            sample_loss[perm[i * bs : (i + 1) * bs]] = losses
            step += 1''')
open(p,'w').write(s)

+H2.6 (supported, c=0.70): Truncating the backward pass at the high-resolution stem cuts per-step cost far more than its FLOP share, at little accuracy cost if the stem has trained at 32 px. Evidence: freezing group 1 and the whitening bias for the last 25% of steps saved ~23% per frozen 32 px step (E043: 7.7 of 33.5 ms, nearly half of it in memory-bound fused kernels) with no held-out loss (E028), and it stacked with +0.5 epoch (E034). Detaching the whitening output after 20% of steps saved a further 2.4% with no held-out loss (E036). Limits: a freeze from 60% cost 0.4–0.56 pp (E037); a conv1-only freeze from 60% saved 0.9% for −0.21 pp (E042); folding frozen group-1 BN saved nothing (E039); a group-2 freeze over the last 10% saved 4.4% for −0.14 pp against a cross-build baseline (E046, inconclusive).

+H2 (supported, c=0.85): At a fixed epoch count, the cost per epoch (systems overhead plus per-layer cost per sample) is a large lever. Levers found so far: compile/fusion (−14%, E004); progressive resizing (−22% E007, −2.9% E026, −3.2% E033); and stem backward truncation, made up of a group-1 freeze over the last 25% of steps (−8.8% with no held-out cost, E028, stacked in E034) and a whitening-bias detach after 20% of steps (−2.4%, E036). Launch overhead is exhausted (E015, E017; Fable's CIFAR-10 record agrees). The E043 profile of the 32 px step (33.5 ms): conv fwd/wgrad/dgrad 66%, memory-bound fused BN/GELU/pointwise 27%, NS plus head ~2.5%. The conv kernels already run at high throughput (H2.2.4), so the remaining per-step levers are the memory-bound share (H6.5) and further backward truncation (H2.6, H6.6). Limits: freezing from 60% costs about 0.4–0.56 pp (E037); folding BN in the frozen phase saves nothing (E039); a group-2 freeze for the last 10% saved 4.4% but read −0.14 pp (E046, inconclusive).

Intermittent stem backward in the 28 px phase, which is the most expensive phase (about 71 steps × ~26 ms ≈ 1.8 s). On the E049 tip, on every second step of the 28 px phase (40–70% of steps), use the group-1-detached 28 px step variant. That variant has no group-1 wgrad/dgrad and no BN/GELU backward on the stem maps, and group-1 params get no Muon/SGD update and no momentum-buffer change on those steps. The variant already existed in E037's commit 6293350. On the other steps, run the usual whitening-detached full step with the group-1 LR as scheduled. Do not rescale the LR: single factor. Group 1 still trains on every step at 20/24 px and from 70% to 75% at 32 px, so it still adapts through the 28→32 switch, which E037/E042 say it needs. Lookahead averages every param. Capture the variant in build with channels_last tensors, with error_on_recompile on. Judge on seeds 13–32 against a same-build E049 baseline, plus seeds 0–2.

import json, statistics as st, math, sys
rows=[json.loads(l) for l in open(sys.argv[1]+'/trials.jsonl')]; acc={r['seed']:r['accuracy'] for r in rows}
t=st.mean(r['total_timed_time'] for r in rows)
h=[acc[s] for s in range(33,53)]; m=st.mean(h); sd=st.stdev(h)
sig=math.sqrt((sd/math.sqrt(20))**2 + sd**2/40 + 0.0005**2)
print("E046 seeds0-2", [acc[s] for s in (0,1,2)], "33-52 mean %.4f sd %.4f lower %.4f pass=%s time %.3f" % (m, sd, m-1.64*sig, m-1.64*sig>=0.75, t))
e049=0.75337; dt=t-5.205
print("vs E049 (0.7534, 5.205 s avg of 4 builds): dacc %.3f pp, dtime %.3f s, dial %.2f s/pp" % (100*(m-e049), dt, dt/(100*(m-e049)) if m!=e049 else float('nan')))
EOF

SEED-OVERFITTING RISK: don't credit gains that only re-roll seeds 0-2 luck; confirm with held-out seeds when a keep hinges on < 0.5 pp.

def train(state) -> nn.Module:
    hyp = state.hyp
    model, opt = state.compiled, state.optimizer
    n, bs = state.n, state.batch_size
    steps_per_epoch = n // bs
    total_steps = math.ceil(hyp["epochs"] * steps_per_epoch)
    schedule = np.interp(
        np.arange(1 + total_steps), [0, int(0.23 * total_steps), total_steps], [0.2, 1.0, 0.07]
    )
    whiten_bias_steps = int(hyp["whiten_bias_frac"] * total_steps)
    # Stem schedule: the same warmup to the peak, then linear to 0 at the freeze point.
    peak = int(0.23 * total_steps)
    freeze_step = int(hyp["freeze_stem_at"] * total_steps) if hyp["freeze_stem_at"] else total_steps + 1
    stem_schedule = np.interp(
        np.arange(1 + total_steps), [0, peak, freeze_step, total_steps + 1], [0.2, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
    )
    g2_step = int(hyp["freeze_g2_at"] * total_steps) if hyp["freeze_g2_at"] else total_steps + 1
    g2_schedule = np.interp(
        np.arange(1 + total_steps),
        [0, freeze_step, g2_step, total_steps + 1],
        [schedule[0], schedule[min(freeze_step, total_steps)], 0.0, 0.0],
    )
    g2_schedule[: freeze_step + 1] = schedule[: freeze_step + 1]
    ema_every = hyp["ema_every"]
    alpha = 0.95**5 * (np.arange(total_steps + 1) / total_steps) ** 3
    lookahead = Lookahead(state.model) if ema_every else None
    # Resolution switches at fixed fractions of the total step count.
    resolution = [
        [r for start, r in hyp["resolutions"] if k >= start * total_steps][-1]
        for k in range(total_steps)
    ]
    step = 0

def make_optimizer(model, hyp, batch_size):
    kilostep_scale = 1024 * (1 + 1 / (1 - hyp["momentum"]))
    lr = hyp["lr"] / kilostep_scale
    wd = hyp["weight_decay"] * batch_size / kilostep_scale
    lr_biases = lr * hyp["bias_scaler"]
    named = [(n, p) for n, p in model.named_parameters() if p.requires_grad]
    stem = lambda n: n.startswith("groups.0.")  # noqa: E731
    g2 = lambda n: n.startswith("groups.1.")  # noqa: E731
    norm_biases = [p for n, p in named if "norm" in n and not stem(n) and not g2(n)]
    g2_norm_biases = [p for n, p in named if "norm" in n and g2(n)]
    g2_filters = [p for n, p in named if p.ndim == 4 and g2(n)]
    stem_norm_biases = [p for n, p in named if "norm" in n and stem(n)]
    whiten_bias = [model.whiten.bias]
    filters = [p for n, p in named if p.ndim == 4 and not stem(n) and not g2(n)]
    stem_filters = [p for n, p in named if p.ndim == 4 and stem(n)]
    other = [p for n, p in named if "norm" not in n and not n.startswith("whiten.") and p.ndim != 4]
    groups = [
        dict(params=norm_biases, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases),
        dict(params=stem_norm_biases, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases, stem=True),
        dict(params=g2_norm_biases, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases, g2=True),
        dict(params=whiten_bias, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases, whiten=True, stem=True),
        dict(params=other, lr=lr, weight_decay=wd / lr),
    ]
    cuda = next(model.parameters()).is_cuda
    sgd = torch.optim.SGD(groups, momentum=hyp["momentum"], nesterov=True, fused=cuda)
    muon = Muon(filters, lr=hyp["muon_lr"], momentum=hyp["muon_momentum"], compiled=cuda)
    stem_muon = Muon(stem_filters, lr=hyp["muon_lr"], momentum=hyp["muon_momentum"], compiled=cuda)
    stem_muon.param_groups[0]["stem"] = True
    g2_muon = Muon(g2_filters, lr=hyp["muon_lr"], momentum=hyp["muon_momentum"], compiled=cuda)
    g2_muon.param_groups[0]["g2"] = True
    opt = Optimizers([sgd, muon, stem_muon, g2_muon])
    for g in opt.param_groups:
        g["base_lr"] = g["lr"]
    return opt

**Tip (E061, 376f231).** E060 with 12 early 20 px steps removed: 225 steps at batch 2000. The 28/32 px phases, the whitening detach and both frozen tails keep their absolute positions. Time is 5.02 s (−0.15 s against E060), almost exactly 12 × 0.016 s minus a little overhead. Accuracy is 0.7534 on seeds 0–2. The population mean is likely about 0.752–0.7525, so meeting the 0.753 local bar is under a coin flip for any change that costs accuracy.

**Noise.**
- Per-seed SD is about 0.3 pp, so a 3-seed SE is about 0.17 pp.
- Time reproduces to about ±0.03 s. Builds can add about 1% to time.
- σ_build appears small (E057), so 40-draw comparisons resolve about 0.1 pp.

**Time model.** Time ≈ 0.25 s + Σ(steps × per-step cost).
- Per-step cost: 32 px 0.032 s, 28 px 0.026 s, 24 px 0.021 s, 20 px 0.016 s.
- A stem-frozen step saves about 8.7 ms; group 2 frozen as well saves about 10 ms more.
- Fixed per-step overhead (three Muon calls with Newton–Schulz, Lookahead, launches) is about 1.5–2.5 ms. Of this, Newton–Schulz is about 0.8 ms per step, about 0.18 s per run.
- Removals land at or slightly below the model (E052, E056, E061).

**Exchange rates (s saved per pp lost).**
- Epoch dial: ~0.8.
- ReLU: ~0.46 (bad).
- Stride instead of pool: bad.
- Data selection: about the dial.
- Earlier freezes: cost (E037, E053, E055).
- Early-step trims: about the dial, though E061 read neutral on seeds 0–2.

**Mechanisms.**
1. Accuracy is bought with optimizer steps on layers that are still learning (E041, E045, E053, E054, E055). Truncation is free only after a layer has finished: whitening bias by ~6%, stem by ~75%, group 2 by ~90%.
2. Lookahead is worth about 1 pp and is already tuned (E025, E030).
3. Muon renormalizes filters, so filter wd is inert. BN scale is frozen. Coarse labels are unavailable.
4. GELU's cost is partly compute (E056 saved 4.8%). A tanh/SiLU swap may recover about half of that at small accuracy risk.
5. Muon's gain over SGD is confounded (E006). Under Muon at momentum 0.6, Muon is probably still worth ≥0.3 pp at batch 2000 with this short horizon, but the evidence is weak.

**Lessons from misses.**
- Diagnostics report the tip's numbers, so for those I forecast the tip's distribution.
- Pure removals: shade time down about 3%.
- E059 came in slower than modelled (builds vary by about 1–2%).

**Unsure.**
- SGD vs Muon on CIFAR-100.

+E033: E027 with resolutions 20/24/28/32 at 30/10/30/30% of steps. seeds 0-2: 0.7536, time 5.69 s; held-out 3-12: 0.7526.

+<!-- what the metrics mean in practice: run-to-run noise, what a real difference looks like -->
+- Paired designs (evaluate the same trained weights with/without a post-training change) remove trajectory noise entirely; use them for any change that doesn't alter training (E044).
+- Even with no RNG-stream change, seeds 0-2 can move opposite to the held-out mean (E025: +0.19 vs -0.27 pp). Treat seeds 0-2 differences < 0.3 pp as uninformative in every case.

+- Seeds 0-2 luck is a (seed x RNG-stream) effect: three builds of E017 give seeds 0-2 means 0.7537/0.7541/0.7536 (+-0.03 pp; per-seed values differ since cudagraph builds aren't bit-reproducible) vs held-out 0.7577. Changes that alter random-number consumption (augment, perm, init order) re-roll the ~0.35 pp luck; kernel/build changes barely move it. SEED-OVERFITTING RISK: don't credit gains that only re-roll seeds 0-2 luck; confirm with held-out seeds when a keep hinges on < 0.5 pp.

+- KEY: the seeds 0-2 mean is much noisier than per-seed std suggests. Deviation of the seeds 0-2 mean from the 10-seed held-out mean: E010 +0.08, E016 +0.43, E017 -0.40 pp -> ~0.35 pp std. 3-seed differences < ~0.6 pp are not interpretable. Seed 1 is persistently the lowest. Settle accuracy claims with held-out seeds 3-12 offline (`benchmark.run --seed 3 --n 10`, ~2.5 min).

+- Two thresholds: official safety (P(40-seed mean >= 0.75) >= 95%) needs population >= ~0.7515; the local bar (seeds 0-2 >= 0.753) needs population >= ~0.7535 to pass in >= 50% of builds. E052 (population ~0.7524, 4.99 s) passes the first, failed the second in its one committed build (E058).

+- Across fresh builds each seed's outcome is re-drawn (per-seed corr ~0), but 20-seed means agree to ~0.013 pp: sigma_build ~ 0 for population estimates (E057). A recipe's seeds 0-2 mean is its population mean + ~0.17 pp noise per build; E049 (population ~0.7534) passes the local bar ~55% of builds.
